metaDescription: Six oscillating multi-tools compared on brushless motors, OPM speed range, quick blade change, vibration, LED light and kit contents for flush cuts.
expertTake: The DEWALT 20V MAX XR DCS356D1 is our top pick for a brushless motor, a quick blade change and a kit that includes a battery and charger. The Hammerhead 2.2 amp corded tool is the value pick for a powerful, low cost multi tool with accessories. Skip an oscillating tool as your only cutting tool, because it excels at flush, plunge and detail cuts but is slow for long straight cuts.
introParagraphs: An oscillating multi tool vibrates a flat blade or sanding pad through a small arc at high speed, which lets it cut flush against a surface, plunge into a wall or sand in a tight corner. It is a problem solver for remodelling, trimming door jambs and removing grout.

The tool's value depends on vibration, blade change speed, accessory compatibility and whether it is corded or battery powered. We evaluated six models from the candidate pool using spec sheets, listing details and owner feedback patterns, then ranked them by fit for common jobs. Check our guide on oscillating multi tool uses for more ideas.

products.name: DEWALT 20V MAX XR oscillating tool DCS356D1, brushless, quick blade change, LED, battery and charger

specList.label: Motor
specList.value: Brushless, up to 57 percent more run time than brushed per the listing

products.description:
The DCS356D1 is a brushless 20V MAX XR oscillating tool with a three speed selector, a dual grip variable speed trigger, a quick blade change and an LED light. The kit includes a battery and charger, so you can start working right away.

The listing claims brushless motors deliver up to 57 percent more run time than brushed, which is a maker figure under ideal conditions. A speed selector and variable trigger give control for delicate flush cuts and for aggressive plunge cuts. Against the Milwaukee M18 FUEL, it comes with a battery. Against the Ryobi, it costs more and has a stronger platform.

Use the right blade for the material and let the tool cut at its own speed. Keep the blade clamp clean and tight. Owners often say the quick blade change is the feature that changes how they work, because swapping from a cutting blade to a sanding pad takes seconds instead of a search for a key.
products.bestFor: Remodellers and DIYers who want a complete, capable kit.
pros: Brushless motor with a stated run time gain
Quick blade change saves time on site
Battery and charger included in the kit
3 speed selector and variable trigger give control
cons: Higher price tier than corded tools
Not ideal for long straight cuts

products.description:
The DCS356SD1 is the same style of brushless 20V multi tool as the DCS356D1, supplied with wood cutting blades, sandpaper, a tool bag, a battery and a charger. The accessories turn it into a ready to go kit.

For a beginner, accessories matter, because blades and sandpaper are the first things you need and cost extra otherwise. The tool shares the three speed selector and dual grip trigger of the DCS356D1. Against the DCS356D1, it adds a bag and accessories. Against the Hammerhead, it adds a battery platform.

Store the accessories in the bag and replace blades as they dull. Remove the battery when changing blades. The tool bag is more useful than it sounds, because loose blades are easily lost in a toolbox and a labelled bag keeps them sorted.

products.name: Milwaukee 2836-20 M18 FUEL brushless oscillating multi tool, tool only
products.description:
The Milwaukee 2836-20 is a brushless M18 FUEL oscillating tool sold as a tool only, with a variable speed dial, an auto load feature that starts slowly for precise cuts and ramps up automatically, and a 180 degree LED light. It is a pro oriented tool.

The auto load feature helps start a cut cleanly without the blade skipping, and the wide LED lights up the work in dark spaces. It is a bare tool, so you need an M18 battery and charger. Against the DEWALT kits, it costs more and targets heavy use. Against the Milwaukee 2626-20, it has a brushless motor.

Use sharp blades and keep the vents clear. Store batteries at partial charge. Contractors say the slow start helps when you begin a flush cut on a painted trim edge, because the blade does not skate along the surface.
pros: Brushless FUEL motor for heavy use
Auto load slow start helps precise cuts
180 degree LED lights the work
Compatible with the M18 battery system
cons: Tool only means batteries are extra

products.name: Milwaukee 2626-20 M18 orbiting multi tool, 11,000 to 18,000 OPM, 12 speeds, bare tool

specList.label: Best for
specList.value: Tough use on a budget for M18 owners

products.description:
The Milwaukee 2626-20 is an older style brushed M18 tool with 12 speed settings from 11,000 to 18,000 orbits per minute and an all metal gear case. A rubberized handle improves grip and the tool comes as a bare unit.

An all metal gear case resists impact damage, which is a durability feature that suits job site use. It uses a brushed motor, so runtime and efficiency are lower than the brushless models. Against the FUEL model, it costs less. If you already own M18 batteries and want a rugged, simple tool, it is a good fit.

Use sharp blades and keep the tool clean. Replace brushes if the motor loses power. If you tend to drop tools on a site, the metal gear case is the sort of feature that keeps a tool alive for years.
products.bestFor: M18 owners who want a rugged, simple multi tool.
pros: 12 speed settings give broad control
All metal gear case resists impacts
Rubberized handle improves grip
Lower price tier than the FUEL model
cons: Tool only means batteries are extra

products.name: RYOBI ONE+ 18V cordless oscillating multi tool, up to 20,000 OPM, tool only

specList.label: Vibration
specList.value: Described as lowest in its class

products.description:
The RYOBI ONE+ multi tool has a variable speed dial up to 20,000 OPM, a design the listing describes as the lowest vibration in its class and a bare tool format for the ONE+ 18V platform. It targets homeowners and DIYers.

Low vibration reduces fatigue on long sanding or scraping jobs. The listing comparison is a maker claim. A low price and a broad battery platform make it a sensible add for existing ONE+ owners. Against the DEWALT kits, it costs less but needs a battery. Against the Hammerhead, it is cordless.

Use the right accessories for the material. Keep the tool clean. Owners who sand for a long time tend to value low vibration more than peak speed, since fatigue ends the job before the battery does.
products.bestFor: Homeowners who already use the RYOBI ONE+ battery platform.

Low vibration design per the listing
Low price tier on a broad platform

products.name: Hammerhead 2.2 amp corded oscillating multi tool, 20,000 OPM, flush cut blade and accessories

specList.label: Included
specList.value: Flush cut blade, semicircle blade, sanding pad and more

products.description:
The Hammerhead is a corded 2.2 amp oscillating tool with a variable speed dial up to 20,000 OPM and a set of accessories that includes a flush cut blade, a semicircle blade and a sanding pad. A corded tool has unlimited runtime and costs far less than a cordless system.

A cord is the tradeoff, as it can catch on the work and limit range. For a workshop or occasional DIY jobs near an outlet, it offers a lot for the price. Against the cordless DEWALT kits, it costs less but lacks freedom. Against the RYOBI, it includes accessories and needs no battery.

Use a rated extension cord and keep the cord away from the blade. Replace accessories as they dull. Because the kit includes a few blades, it is a good way to try an oscillating tool before deciding to commit to a battery platform.

buyingCriteria.explanation: A brushless motor is more efficient, runs cooler and lasts longer than a brushed one. The DEWALT and Milwaukee FUEL tools are brushless, and the Milwaukee 2626-20, RYOBI and Hammerhead are brushed in these listings. Brushless matters most for cordless tools, where efficiency means runtime. See our guide on brushed versus brushless motors. The usual buyer mistake is spending on a tool and then using cheap blades, which cut slowly and make the tool feel weak.

OPM is oscillations per minute. The Milwaukee 2626-20 runs 11,000 to 18,000 and the RYOBI and Hammerhead go to 20,000. A lower speed suits delicate work and a high speed suits cutting. A speed dial gives control. Think about which accessories you will need: a flush cut blade, a scraper and a sanding pad cover most jobs.

Oscillating tools vibrate your hand, and long jobs tire you. Low vibration designs, like the RYOBI, a rubberized grip like the Milwaukee and a dual grip trigger like the DEWALT help. Test the feel if you can. Check how the dust is cleared, since sanding with an oscillating pad creates fine dust that a vacuum adapter helps to control.

A quick blade change saves time and a universal mounting accepts blades from many brands. Check that the tool accepts the accessories you plan to use. A tool free clamp is more convenient than a hex key. Consider the weight of the tool with a battery fitted, as a heavy tool is tiring on overhead cuts.

Choose a platform you already own. DEWALT 20V MAX, Milwaukee M18 and RYOBI ONE+ are popular. Several listings here are bare tools, so budget for a battery and charger. See our guide on battery voltage and amp hours. Look at the shape of the nose and the position of the LED, because shadows hide the cut line in tight spots.

Accessories matter for a first purchase. The DEWALT DCS356SD1 includes blades, sandpaper and a bag, and the Hammerhead includes a flush cut blade, semicircle blade and sanding pad. A bare tool needs separate accessories. Keep spare blades handy, since a dull blade is the commonest reason people think their tool is underpowered.

howWeEvaluated.title: Motor and efficiency
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared brushless and brushed motors and the stated run time gain on the DEWALT. We treated maker claims as best case figures and did not cut with the tools. Owner feedback patterns about vibration, blade clamp wear and battery runtime shaped our scoring.

howWeEvaluated.title: Speed control
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at speed ranges from 11,000 to 20,000 OPM and selectors or dials. Wider control scored higher. We treated stated run time gains as maker claims under ideal conditions.

howWeEvaluated.title: Comfort and vibration
howWeEvaluated.description: We weighed grips and vibration claims on the RYOBI and Milwaukee. Lower vibration scored higher. Where a listing was a bare tool we treated the battery as part of the real price.

howWeEvaluated.title: Kit and platform
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered included batteries, accessories and platform breadth. Total cost mattered. We compared how many accessories each kit includes and what they are.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ownership
howWeEvaluated.description: We reviewed gear case durability, blade clamp wear and owner feedback patterns. Established brands scored higher. Platform breadth was weighed because most buyers add tools over time. Owners of cheaper tools often mention that accessories are the real running cost, which we considered in the value ranking. Safety matters too, so we noted any listing that omitted a mention of blade guards or accessory compatibility.

maintenance.why: A dull blade strains the motor and cuts poorly. Replace when teeth dull. Put a drop of oil on the clamp lever every few months.
Dust and debris jam the clamp. Blow it out. Check the pad for cracks.
Dust overheats the motor. Use compressed air. Wipe the vents.
Cracks and play lead to failure. Replace worn parts. Use a small brush to clear the clamp.

Heat shortens battery life. Store at partial charge. Keep accessories in a labelled bag. Store the accessories in the labelled bag so blades stay sharp and do not rust, which keeps a good kit useful for years.

faq.q: What can I do with an oscillating multi tool?
faq.a: Flush cuts, plunge cuts, sanding in corners, grout removal and scraping. Our guide on oscillating multi tool uses covers many jobs. Many owners say a few quality blades are the best investment, because the right blade makes any tool feel better.
For a cordless tool, yes, since efficiency stretches runtime. For occasional use, brushed is fine. Hold the tool firmly with both hands for plunge cuts and let the blade reach full speed first.
Many tools accept universal blades, but check the mount of your tool. Brand specific mounts exist. Use a low speed for scraping and a higher speed for cutting wood and plastic.
A dull blade, forcing the tool or a loose clamp. Let the blade do the work at its own speed. Wear eye protection and a dust mask, because the tool throws fine dust and debris.
Corded has unlimited runtime and costs less. Cordless offers freedom and suits remodelling. Clamp the workpiece or hold it firmly, since vibration makes loose pieces move.

Yes, with a bi metal or carbide blade, at slower speed. Check the blade rating for the metal. Tap the blade clamp clean now and then, because dust builds up and makes blade changes harder. Practise on scrap material before cutting a finished surface, since a plunge cut at speed can slip and mark the surface around it.
